courses.subject: COMP
courses.title: Information Visualization
courses.description: Data is everywhere. Charts, graphs, and other types of information visualizations help people to make sense of data. This course explores the design, development, and evaluation of these visualizations. By combining aspects of design, computer graphics, HCI, and data science, you will gain hands-on experience with creating visualizations, using exploratory tools, and architecting data narratives. Topics include interactive systems, user-centered design, graphical perception and cognition, data storytelling, and insight building. Throughout this course, you will work directly with stakeholders to analyze data from a variety of domains and applications.

source.text: COMP 616. | 3 Credits.

courses.subject: COMP
courses.title: Visualization Design Methods
courses.description: Data visualization combines computational, design, and cognitive principles to help people explore, communicate, and analyze large datasets. Developing effective visualizations often requires working closely with interdisciplinary teams to authentically reflect the needs of a data problem. This course will provide a hands-on introduction to common design methods for creating visualizations in different domains and problem constraints. Students will work with a variety of datasets to generate visualization solutions leveraging various design methodologies and media. Topics will include data sketching and crafting, user-centered design, task-driven design, cognitively-driven design, quantitative and qualitative experimental methods, and workshop methods.

courses.subject: COMP
courses.title: Formal Methods for System Security
courses.description: Formal methods provide a rigorous, mathematically grounded analysis of a system. Used as part of a security analysis, formal methods can provide verification that a system meets its security requirements. In this course students will learn about and gain experience using a variety of techniques, including symbolic execution, model checking, and proofs of equivalence and refinement. Students will develop an understanding of different specification logics and what can and cannot be expressed in each. Topics include assertion-based verification, simulation relations, linear temporal logic, information flow analysis, and hyperproperties.

courses.subject: COMP
courses.title: Stochastic Performance Modeling and Evaluation of Computer Systems
courses.description: Fundamentals of stochastic performance modeling of computer systems. This course builds a foundation in the stochastic processes used to model modern computer systems, and develops theoretical techniques for analyzing these models. Students will use these tools to answer practical questions such as: How can we minimize latency or maximize throughput in a system? How many servers do I need to buy to meet my latency/throughput goals? Should I buy one faster server, or two slower servers? How should I balance load across the many servers in my system? What is the optimal scheduling policy for my system?

courses.description: Over the last few years, the field of AI has been revolutionized by the emergence of transformer models. In this course, we will study transformer models for various computer vision problems. The course will consist of research paper presentations, interactive exercises, research paper discussions, and a semester-long course project. Topics will include transformer architectures for images and videos, efficient transformer model design, data-efficient learning, self-supervised learning, multimodal learning, image generation, and others. This course is a semester-long 3-credit course, appropriate for graduate students and advanced undergraduate students with an interest in applying transformer models to computer vision.

Topics include syntactic parsing, co-reference resolution, semantic parsing, question answering, document summarization, machine translation, dialogue models, and multi-modality.

courses.subject: COMP
courses.title: Technical Communication in Computer Science
courses.description: This course for doctoral students covers aspects of written and oral technical communication in computer science, including public speaking, writing, posters, and social networking. The course frames all communication as a teaching exercise, and includes a short lesson and peer critiques of the lesson. The course also introduces students to the business and administrative aspects of building a teaching or research career, as well as how to navigate common interpersonal and organizational challenges in research.
